issues.legal_issue: A person holding inam land at the commencement of the land-revenue regime automatically acquired the new tenure status, with the statutory reference to land held identifying the holder’s status and character in relation to the land at that time.
material_facts: The land was held as inam land when the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code came into force.
The person holding the inam land at that time was recognized as the inamdar.
issues.conclusion: The inam rights were extinguished and the person holding the land as inamdar automatically acquired bhumiswami status and the rights and liabilities attached to that status.
issues.legal_principle: Section 158(1)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 extinguished inam rights and conferred bhumiswami status on every person holding land as an inamdar when the Code came into force. The words “in respect of land held by him” refer to the status and character of the tenure holder in relation to the holding on that date; the status accrued automatically.

predicates.tenure_conversion_dispute: The proceeding concerns the legal effect of a statutory change to a land tenure.
predicates.person_held_inam_land_at_conversion: A person held the land under the former tenure when the new land regime took effect.

issues.definition: When a tenure-conversion dispute concerns land held by a person under the former tenure when the new regime takes effect, that holder automatically acquires the new tenure status.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory conversion of ancestral inam land extinguishes its incidents of impartibility and primogeniture, and the new tenure benefits the joint family when the land was joint family property.
material_facts: The inam land had descended within the family under a grant that made it impartible and subject to succession by lineal primogeniture.
The family treated the inam land and property acquired from its income as joint family property.
The land was held as inam land when the new tenure regime took effect.
issues.conclusion: The conversion removed the restrictions of impartibility and primogeniture, and the new tenure rights enured to the benefit of the joint family; the land could be held in joint ownership and partitioned as coparcenary property.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 158(1)(b) and 164 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, read together, extinguished the inam tenure and its incidents of impartibility and primogeniture. The interests of a bhumiswami pass subject to personal law by inheritance, survivorship or bequest. Applying Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai, the statutory change in tenure does not destroy pre-existing joint-family rights, and the new rights enure to the benefit of the joint family.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.ancestral_inam_was_joint_family_property: The inam land was ancestral property treated and held within the family as joint family property.
predicates.tenure_restrictions_were_removed: A change in the land tenure removed restrictions that had made the land impartible and governed its devolution by primogeniture.

issues.definition: If a partition proceeding concerns ancestral inam land that was joint family property and the tenure restrictions have been removed, the converted land benefits the joint family and is partitionable.

issues.legal_issue: The impartibility of an ancestral estate and succession by primogeniture do not by themselves end the joint-family character of the estate or the right of survivorship; ending that status requires proof that junior family members intended to renounce succession.
material_facts: The inam estate was ancestral, impartible and devolved under a rule of lineal primogeniture.
The evidence showed that the family treated the estate and property acquired from its income as joint family property.
The trial court found that the alleged partition had not occurred, and that finding was not reversed.
The record did not establish that the junior members had renounced their right of succession.
issues.conclusion: The estate retained its character as joint family property, with survivorship governed by the applicable rule of succession; impartibility alone did not make it the separate property of the holder.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, an ancestral estate does not become the holder’s separate property merely because it is impartible: custom may displace ordinary incidents of joint property, but survivorship remains unless renounced. Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai reaffirmed that principle. To establish that a Mitakshara family holding an impartible estate has ceased to be joint, an express or implied intention by junior members to renounce succession must be proved.

predicates.ancestral_impartible_estate_dispute: The proceeding concerns an ancestral estate that is impartible under its governing custom or grant.
predicates.estate_descended_within_family: The estate passed among members of the family under a succession rule applicable to the family estate.
predicates.junior_members_did_not_renounce_successi: The junior family members did not expressly or impliedly give up their right to succeed to the estate.

issues.definition: When an ancestral impartible estate passes within a family and junior members have not renounced succession, the estate remains joint family property with survivorship.
